> 賁。亨。小利有攸往。

Hexagram 22 is about ornament, and its character has been misread as a picture in every generation that liked the picture.

## 賁 is 從貝，卉聲

說文: 賁，飾也。從貝，卉聲.

A phonetic compound: 貝 as the semantic side (shells were valuable ornament), 卉 as the sound.

Original sense: ornament, decoration. The name is read bì.

(虎賁's 賁 is bēn, "a warrior" — a different word entirely, and not this one.)

This is the fourth of its kind in this series: 訟 從言公聲, 謙 從言兼聲, 觀 從見雚聲, 賁 從貝卉聲. Four instances is no longer an accident; it is a habit of the commentary tradition. When a phonetic compound happens to have components that suggest a meaning, the reader starts calling it 會意, and the reading produced is always smoother than the truth.

## 白賁, and the direction of the whole hexagram

The top line is three characters: 白賁，無咎 — white ornament.

Decoration that has arrived at plainness, and the verdict is no fault.

Which is the shape of the hexagram: it moves from ornamenting the feet, to ornamenting the beard, to something washed, to the plain ground, and ends at white.

So 賁 is not condemned. It is graded, and the top of the grade is an ornament that has thinned to nothing.

## 須: the beard hangs from the face

六二 賁其須.

須 is the beard, which hangs on the jaw and cannot exist apart from it.

The 象 supplies the reading: 文 cannot stand by itself. Ornament attaches to substance the way a beard attaches to a chin.

Which is a much better argument than "decoration is superficial." The beard is real; it is also entirely dependent. That is the exact position the hexagram assigns to 文.

## 舍車而徒

初九 賁其趾，舍車而徒.

To ornament the foot — and to leave the carriage and walk.

The lowest line chooses the plainest form of motion and refuses the vehicle. Which the text does not treat as a deprivation. The feet are being ornamented; walking is the ornament.

## 皤如, 翰如

說文: 皤，老人白也 — white, pale, the white of age.

翰如 — glossed either as the swiftness of a horse or as its whiteness. A white horse, plain, not decked.

六四: 賁如，皤如，白馬翰如；匪寇，婚媾.

Ornament, and then paleness; a white horse; not a raider, a marriage.

The line is the hexagram's turn: what approaches looks like a threat because it is unadorned, and it is actually the union.

## 束帛戋戋

六五 賁于丘園，束帛戋戋，吝，終吉.

丘園: hill and garden — the plain country, away from the city's finish.

戋戋: slight, meagre (釋文 cites 子夏's text as 殘殘, also "thin"). A small bundle of silk.

The gift is thin, the ceremony is reduced, and the verdict is 吝 and then 終吉.

So the hexagram says out loud what most ceremonial writing avoids: a thin offering looks bad at the moment it is made, and it is correct.

(Another reading takes 戋戋 as "piled up, abundant." This book takes the thin reading, because 吝，終吉 requires something to be regretted at first.)

## 剛柔交錯，天文也

This clause is missing from the transmitted draft and has been restored to the base text.

The interleaving of firm and yielding is 天文 — the pattern of sky, sun, moon, stars. And 人文 is the corresponding human pattern: rites, order, ceremony.

So ornament is not invented. It is the same structure found twice, once above and once in human arrangement.

## 明庶政，無敢折獄

The 象's limit: fire illuminates the affairs of government, which suits orderly administration — and ornament must not be used to decide cases.

折獄 needs plainness. A decorated argument is a way of covering the truth, and the chapter that has just spent five lines praising ornament forbids it in exactly one place.

Which is the discipline of the hexagram: 文 can order anything except the finding of fact.

## The test

Take the presentation you are currently polishing — a deck, a paper, a way of explaining yourself. Ask which line you are on. The first line leaves the carriage and walks; the top line arrives at white. Both are ornament. Neither is absence.
